name: AFDD (Arc Fault Detection Device)
tagline: Listens for the crackle of a bad connection — and trips before the arc becomes a fire.
terminals: L in / N in (top) — supply from the MCB or RCBO upstream
L out / N out (bottom) — the protected final circuit
Functional earth / neutral fly-lead on some designs
parts: Microprocessor — samples current and looks for the arc signature
Series and parallel arc detection — broken conductor vs L-to-N tracking
Tripping relay — opens both poles on a detected arc
safety: An AFDD does not replace an MCB or an RCD — it is normally an AFDD-RCBO that combines all three in one module. Never fit one to defeat nuisance tripping: repeated arc trips are telling you a connection, a flex or an accessory is breaking down, and that fault needs finding.

points.label: L / N in (top)
points.detail: Supply comes in at the top from the protective device upstream. An AFDD is always fed from an overcurrent device — it senses arcs but is not rated to clear a short-circuit on its own.

points.label: Toggle lever
points.detail: Switches both poles together. On most designs the lever sits midway when the device has tripped on a fault, which is your first clue that the trip was automatic rather than someone switching it off.

points.label: Test button 'T'
points.detail: Injects a simulated arc signature so the internal electronics and the tripping relay are exercised end to end. Test it on the same schedule as the RCD test button — a few times a year, and record the result.

points.label: Arc-detection electronics
points.detail: The device samples the current waveform continuously and looks for the tell-tale pattern of a series arc: a flat spot at each zero crossing, broadband noise, and irregular half-cycles that a normal load such as a dimmer or a motor does not produce. That discrimination is what keeps it from tripping on ordinary switching.

points.label: Front face and housing
points.detail: One module wide (about 18 mm) on a modern AFDD-RCBO, or two on older combined units. The label carries the ratings you must record on the schedule: In, the 30 mA RCD marking, the type (AC, A, F or B), and the breaking capacity.

points.label: L / N out (bottom)
points.detail: The protected circuit leaves here. Both live and neutral pass through the device, because the neutral current is part of the signature it analyses — a borrowed or shared neutral downstream will usually cause it to trip.

points.label: DIN-rail clip
points.detail: Spring-loaded foot for the 35 mm rail. With the busbar and the neutral fly-lead both connected, unclipping the device takes real care: release it slowly and support the conductors.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of an AFDD arc fault detection device showing the microprocessor board, arc-sensing transformer, filtering and the tripping relay

cutawayPoints.label: Arc-sensing transformer
cutawayPoints.detail: A wideband current transformer around the live conductor, listening for the high-frequency content an arc puts on the waveform. A normal load is smooth at those frequencies; a loose terminal sparking is not. This is the input the rest of the device works from — no sensing, no detection.

cutawayPoints.label: Filtering and power supply
cutawayPoints.detail: The front end that conditions what the sensor hears and powers the electronics from the circuit being protected. It has to do both from a few millivolts of signal on a conductor carrying a kettle, a dimmer or a switched-mode supply, which is why an AFDD is far more than an RCD with a chip bolted on.

cutawayPoints.label: Microprocessor
cutawayPoints.detail: Samples the current continuously and looks for the shape of an arc rather than its size: the current zero period, the erratic burst-to-burst variation, the broadband noise. That signature is what separates a bad connection sparking from a dimmer or a motor brush doing the same thing harmlessly — and getting it wrong is what used to make early AFDDs nuisance-trip.

cutawayPoints.label: Tripping relay
cutawayPoints.detail: The device cannot open the circuit with a semiconductor, so detection ends here: a relay driven by the processor opens both poles. It is a protective device first, so the relay is the part that has to interrupt a fault current, not just signal one.

cutawayPoints.label: Test button
cutawayPoints.detail: Injects a waveform that mimics an arc so the whole chain — sensor, filtering, processor, relay — is exercised rather than just the electronics. It proves the device still detects; it does not prove anything about the wiring downstream, which is where the arcs it is looking for actually start.

cutawayPoints.label: Line and neutral terminals
cutawayPoints.detail: In at the top, out at the bottom, like any other DIN-rail device. The difference is what is behind them: an AFDD is often specified per circuit on a board where the cables are long and the terminations are the most likely thing in the installation to work loose — which is exactly the fault it exists to catch.
